what_it_does: Approximate nearest-neighbor search (ANNS) is the database operation that finds the stored vectors (lists of numbers representing, say, images or sentences) closest to a query vector — it is the backbone of recommendation systems, image search, and retrieval-augmented AI. The bottleneck is that the database is enormous and lives in large off-chip memory chips; the processor must fetch many candidate vectors, compute a distance score for each, and then throw most of them away as too far from the query. ANSMET tackles both wasteful fetching and wasteful computation by moving the distance calculation directly into hardware units sitting inside the memory chips themselves (called near-data processing — doing arithmetic right where the data lives). Before a vector is fully loaded, ANSMET computes a guaranteed lower bound on its distance using only the first few dimensions or the most significant bits of each number; if that lower bound is already larger than the best distance seen so far, it stops loading and discards the vector immediately, saving both memory traffic and computation.
